2026 ACCP/ASHP Critical Care Pharmacy Specialty Review Course Practice Exam

Before viewing the test, please read and agree to the statement below.

Next  
 You are able to access the test before its start date of  because you are an ACCP staff member.
  •   Instructions
  •   Questions
  •   Summary

Instructions

How to Use the ACCP/ASHP Critical Care Pharmacy Specialty Review Course Practice Exam:

  1. Take the online practice exam as a diagnostic tool to identify knowledge gaps.
  2. Obtain a score.
  3. Click View Practice Exam to obtain the answer rationale document. The rationale document includes correct answers and corresponding rationales, reference sources, and the domains, tasks, and knowledge statements.
  4. Click Retake Practice Exam to access the practice exam as many times as you wish.
    (If you opt to retake the practice exam, please print the rationale/answers document as your answers will not be saved for future reference.)

Helpful hints:

  • You may return to a question and change your answer any time before submitting the practice exam.
  • You may save a partially completed practice exam and return at a later time.
  • Be sure to submit your practice exam when you are finished, so that you can view the answers.
  Product        Save & Exit      Next  

Questions

Practice Standards, Training, and Professional Development

*Question 1:

Which best depicts the medical complication for which a higher mortality rate in ICUs without clinical pharmacists, compared with ICUs with clinical pharmacists, has been documented?

  A.

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

  B.

Cardiogenic shock.

  C.

Traumatic brain injury (TBI).

  D.

Thromboembolic and infarction-related events.

*Question 2:

A 24-year-old man is admitted to the trauma ICU after a motor vehicle collision. Major injuries include a severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and multiple rib fractures. His medical history is unremarkable. Social history is significant for daily vaping. The patient is placed on a mechanical ventilator. Which most accurately represents the core knowledge base most needed by a pharmacist to directly assist with this patient’s acute care?

  A.

Pulmonary disease.

  B.

Infectious disease.

  C.

Neurology.

  D.

Nephrology.

*Question 3:

In level 1 critical care centers, which critical care pharmacy service has the largest number of standards and recommendations after the Patient Care category?

  A.

Quality Improvement.

  B.

Research/Scholarship.

  C.

Training/Education.

  D.

Professional Development.

*Question 4:

Which best depicts the association that has not formed critical care pharmacist specialty groups?

  A.

Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM).

  B.

American College of Clinical Pharmacy (ACCP).

  C.

Neurocritical Care Society (NCS).

  D.

American Society of Health-System Pharmacists (ASHP).

*Question 5:

According to a national survey conducted in 2018, which best represents the percentage of institutions with direct clinical ICU services?

  A.

60%.

  B.

70%.

  C.

80%.

  D.

90%.

*Question 6:

Which best describes the obligation of the employer, as a stakeholder in the critical care pharmacist’s continuing professional development, to ensure continued professional growth?

  A.

Reimbursement for continuing professional education events.

  B.

Funding of travel to at least one national meeting every other year.

  C.

Promotion and support of an environment that encourages sharing and learning.

  D.

Establishment of a formal mentoring program for all pharmacists.

*Question 7:

Of the 5 principles of team‐based health care defined in the Institute of Medicine (now the National Institute of Medicine) 2012 discussion paper on the principles and values of effective team-based health care, which is most challenging to implement and maintain by many critical care teams?

  A.

Measures of team performance.

  B.

Clear delineation of roles.

  C.

Common treatment goals.

  D.

Mutual trust.

Research Design and Biostatistics

*Question 8:

A clinical trial will evaluate treatment strategies for refractory alcohol withdrawal in critically ill patients. The study will seek to determine whether lorazepam equivalencies are reduced by valproic acid intravenous boluses, dexmedetomidine continuous infusion, or phenobarbital intravenous boluses. The team consulted the institutional review board and institutional ethics committee to identify relevant ethical issues within the trial design. Which trial design issue is most relevant to the ethical conduct of this study?

  A.

Uninformative study population.

  B.

Lack of clinical equipoise between treatment arms for the primary outcome.

  C.

Inability to blind study drugs.

  D.

Ability to obtain informed consent from participants with altered mental status.

*Question 9:

Recent studies of patients with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) show a 50% incidence of the composite outcome of death or major disability in the standard treatment arm. This is decreased from historical estimates of 65%–70% for death or major disability in patients with ICH because standard of care has improved in clinical trials and epidemiologic studies. The investigators of a new clinical trial are evaluating the effectiveness of a novel drug compound to promote hemostasis in anticoagulated vs nonanticoagulated patients. This drug has already shown impressive results for all subtypes of ICH. Which is the best consideration for study design?

  A.

The study will need a larger sample size than historical trials to obtain statistical power.

  B.

The study will need a smaller sample size than historical trials to obtain statistical power.

  C.

The trial should limit study inclusion to patients with only subdural hematoma to decrease the likelihood of a type I error.

  D.

The trial should limit study inclusion to patients with only subdural hematoma to decrease the likelihood of a type II error.

*Question 10:

You are conducting the statistical analysis for a pharmacy resident research project. The study includes mechanically ventilated patients who are initiated on propofol immediately after intubation compared with those who are initiated on dexmedetomidine as the sole sedative agent. The primary outcome is the patient’s Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) score (range, –5 to 4) at 48 hours after propofol or dexmedetomidine initiation. Which test is most appropriate to use?

  A.

Mann-Whitney U test for ordinal data.

  B.

Student t test for continuous data.

  C.

Wilcoxon signed rank test for ordinal data.

  D.

Paired t test for continuous data.

*Question 11:

An epidemiologic study seeks to evaluate the impact of hyperammonemia on altered mentation in critically ill patients treated with valproic acid, which has an estimated incidence of up to 52% in this population. Which is the best design for this study?

  A.

Prospective observational study using time-to-event analysis to evaluate difference in development of altered mental status in those who did and did not have hyperammonemia.

  B.

Retrospective case-control study with statistical analysis for proportions to determine difference in altered mental status in those who did and did not have hyperammonemia.

  C.

Randomized controlled trial using chi-square and logistic regression analyses to determine difference in altered mental status in those who did and did not have hyperammonemia.

  D.

Retrospective cohort study with statistical analysis for proportions to determine difference in altered mental status in those who did and did not have hyperammonemia.

*Question 12:

A cohort study was conducted to determine whether low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) used for venous thromboembolism was associated with an increased rate of significant bleeding compared with unfractionated heparin. The final statistical analysis for clinically significant bleeding with LMWH showed an odds ratio (OR) of 0.92 (95% CI, 0.86–0.95). Which best describes the results?

  A.

Use of LMWH increased the odds of clinically significant bleeding by 8%.

  B.

Use of LMWH was not associated with an increase or decrease in clinically significant bleeding.

  C.

Use of LMWH decreased the odds of clinically significant bleeding by 5%.

  D.

Use of LMWH decreased the odds of clinically significant bleeding by 8%.

*Question 13:

A recent study evaluated the rates of acute kidney injury (AKI) with 3 different drugs that lower blood pressure in patients with hypertensive crisis. Results showed that 28% of patients developed AKI with drug A, 37% with drug B, and 56% with drug C. Which best depicts the number needed to harm (NNH) for drug B compared with drug A?

  A.

3.

  B.

6.

  C.

11.

  D.

Cannot be calculated.

*Question 14:

A recent study randomized critically ill patients with sepsis to β-lactam therapy by continuous infusion vs intermittent bolus to evaluate intensive care unit–free days at 28 days, clinical and microbiological cure at 14 days, and 90-day survival. The study disproportionately enrolled more patients with susceptible organisms showing lower minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) than patients with resistant organisms (higher MICs). Results showed no difference for any outcomes between the two treatment arms. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modeling data have shown higher pharmacodynamic target attainment with continuous infusions than with intermittent bolus therapy. Which best describes why continuous infusion therapy can still be considered for use in critically ill patients with sepsis, according to these study results?

  A.

Continuous infusion therapy should not be considered because this study failed to show a significant difference between study groups, and practical difficulties with continuous infusion outweigh any potential clinical benefit.

  B.

This study likely had selection bias. Patients with resistant organisms are more likely to benefit from continuous infusions, but this group was not adequately represented in the study. These patients may be at high risk of therapeutic failure with intravenous bolus administration.

  C.

Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic models do not adequately represent patient-specific populations and should not be used for dosing considerations in unique populations.

  D.

This study should have been designed as a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study in agreement with previous data that have been generated to further explore the usefulness of continuous infusions vs more traditional intravenous bolus approaches.

Fluids, Electrolytes, Acid-Base Disorders, and Nutrition

The next four questions pertain to the following case.

A.A., a 34-year-old man (height 172.7 cm, weight 87 kg) with no significant medical history, was admitted to the trauma intensive care unit with multiple gunshot wounds that injured his small bowel and colon. He initially underwent jejunal and transverse colon resections for repair, but his postoperative course was complicated by a prolonged ileus. A.A.’s nasogastric output was 5.9 L over the past 24 hours, and his laboratory values this morning are significant for sodium 142 mEq/L, chloride 98 mEq/L, and bicarbonate (HCO3) 35 mEq/L. His arterial blood gas (ABG) shows pH 7.47, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (Pco2) 50 mm Hg, and HCO3 36 mEq/L. 

*Question 15:

Which most accurately describes A.A.’s acid-base disorder(s)?

  A.

Anion gap (AG) metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

  B.

Non-AG metabolic acidosis with concurrent metabolic alkalosis.

  C.

Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation.

  D.

Metabolic alkalosis with concurrent respiratory alkalosis.

*Question 16:

A.A.’s course is later complicated by a small bowel fistula with an average output of 1 L/d despite bowel rest. His intravenous fluid order is for 0.45% sodium chloride at 75 mL/h. His laboratory values today include sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 4 mEq/L, chloride 92 mEq/L, bicarbonate 16 mEq/L, serum urea nitrogen (SUN) 51 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.72 mg/dL, and lactate 4.2 Mg/dL. His most recent vital signs are notable for pulse rate 115 beats/minute and blood pressure 92/50 mm Hg. His urine output over the past 24 hours was 720 mL. Which change to A.A.’s intravenous fluid regimen would be best?

  A.

Continue 0.45% sodium chloride and increase the rate to 150 mL/h.

  B.

Administer a 1-L bolus of 0.45% sodium chloride and continue 0.45% sodium chloride at 75 mL/h.

  C.

Administer a 1-L bolus of lactated Ringer solution and change fluids to lactated Ringer solution at 150 mL/h.

  D.

Administer a 1-L bolus of lactated Ringer solution and change fluids to 0.45% sodium chloride at 125 mL/h.

*Question 17:

A.A.’s arterial blood gas shows pH 7.31, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (Pco2) 46 mm Hg, and bicarbonate (HCO3) 18 mEq/L. His laboratory values today include 128 mEq/L, potassium 4 mEq/L, chloride 92 mEq/L, HCO3 16 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 51 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.72 mg/dL, and lactate 4.2 mg/dL. Which most accurately describes his current acid-base disorder(s)? Reference: normal anion gap (AG) = 12 mEq/L

  A.

AG metabolic acidosis and respiratory acidosis

  B.

Non-AG metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis

  C.

AG metabolic acidosis, non-AG metabolic acidosis, and respiratory alkalosis

  D.

AG metabolic acidosis, a non-AG metabolic acidosis, and a respiratory acidosis

*Question 18:

Over the next several days, A.A.’s renal function and vital signs improve. His pertinent laboratory values today are as follows: sodium, 132 mEq/L; potassium, 4.1 mEq/L; serum urea nitrogen, 36 mg/dL; serum creatinine (SCr), 1.01 mg/dL; phosphate (PO4), 1.6 mg/dL; and magnesium, 1.1 mg/dL. His urine output has increased to 2100 mL over the past 24 hours. Which plan for A.A.’s electrolyte repletion needs is most appropriate?

  A.

Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously × 2 doses and sodium phosphate 45 mmol intravenously × 1 dose.

  B.

Magnesium sulfate 2 g intravenously × 1 dose and sodium phosphate 15 mmol intravenously × 1 dose.

  C.

Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously × 1 dose and potassium phosphate/sodium phosphate 500 mg orally × 3 doses.

  D.

Magnesium oxide 400 mg orally × 2 doses and potassium phosphate/sodium phosphate 500 mg orally × 3 doses.

The next two questions pertain to the following case.

C.A., a 50-year-old man (height 152.4 cm, weight 33 kg) with a 3-month history of watery diarrhea, frequent vomiting with oral intake, and an 18-kg weight loss, is admitted to the medical intensive care unit (ICU) because of hypovolemic shock. His imaging reveals a large obstructing rectal mass of concern for malignancy and significant thickening of the colonic wall consistent with colitis. 

*Question 19:

After volume resuscitation is complete and hemodynamic stability is achieved on ICU day 2, the team asks for your recommendation on the route of nutrition for this patient. Which is the most appropriate recommendation for C.A.’s nutrition at this time? 

  A.

Initiate parenteral nutrition (PN) today.

  B.

Initiate enteral nutrition (EN) today.

  C.

Initiate both EN and PN today.

  D.

Try to provide EN today, and initiate PN in 7 to 10 days if he does not tolerate EN.

*Question 20:

On intensive care unit (ICU) day 3, C.A.’s rectal mass prolapsed, and he was taken to surgery to undergo transanal excision of the mass. By day 4, he had enteral nutrition (EN) (1 kcal/mL; protein 64 g/L) infusing through a nasogastric feeding tube at 70 mL/hour. He initially remained in the ICU for severe electrolyte derangements, fever, and tachycardia, though he has now stabilized and remained off vasopressors after surgery. Although he has not had a bowel movement yet, his abdomen is soft, and he has not experienced emesis. Which best assesses C.A.’s nutrition regimen, and which changes would be best to suggest?

  A.

C.A. is not tolerating his feeds. Discontinue EN and begin parenteral nutrition (PN).

  B.

C.A. is tolerating his feeds, but his fluid intake is too high. Change to a 2-kcal/mL EN formula and decrease the rate to 35 mL/h.

  C.

C.A. is tolerating his feeds. Continue the current EN formula and decrease the rate to 40 mL/h.

  D.

C.A. is not tolerating his feeds. Continue the current EN regimen but ask that his feeding tube be advanced to a postpyloric location for better tolerance.

The next two questions pertain to the following case.

D.A., a 47-year-old woman (height 162.6 cm, weight 57 kg) with a history of hypertension and pancreatic adenocarcinoma complicated by a gastric outlet obstruction, was admitted to the surgical intensive care unit after a gastrojejunal bypass and gastrojejunostomy tube placement. Because of her significant bowel edema, she was left in discontinuity and currently has an open abdomen with a wound vacuum in place. The volume of output from her midline wound over the past 24 hours was 2.8 L. Her laboratory values this morning were as follows: sodium, 140 mEq/L; potassium, 3.7 mEq/L; chloride, 100 mEq/L; bicarbonate (HCO3), 23 mEq/L; serum urea nitrogen, 18 mg/dL; serum creatinine, 0.79 mg/dL; and glucose, 101 mg/dL.

*Question 21:

Which protein goal would be most appropriate for D.A.’s nutrition support plan?

  A.

65 g.

  B.

135 g.

  C.

105 g.

  D.

85 g.

*Question 22:

A furosemide infusion was initiated at 15 mg/hour to try to reduce the edema in D.A.’s abdomen before she returned to surgery for abdominal closure. On the day of surgery, her furosemide infusion was discontinued because she was requiring fluid boluses for hypotension and tachycardia. She returned to the surgical intensive care unit after the operation, and her laboratory values were significant for sodium 154 mEq/L. The team would like to correct her serum sodium. Which regimen would best correct D.A.’s sodium?

  A.

5% dextrose in water at 60 mL/hour for 24 hours, then 30 mL/hour for 48 hours.

  B.

5% dextrose in water at 75 mL/hour for the next 48 –72 hours.

  C.

5% dextrose/0.9% sodium chloride 60 mL/hour for 24 hours, then 30 mL/hour for 48 hours.

  D.

5% dextrose/0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL/hour for the next 48 –72 hours.

Protocol Development and Quality Improvement

*Question 23:

The director of pharmacy operations has been tasked with implementing United States Pharmacopeia (USP) 800 standards related to the safe handling of hazardous medications. Which strategy would best assess the current pharmacy workflows for handling hazardous medications compared with USP 800 standards?

  A.

Medication use evaluation (MUE).

  B.

Gap analysis. 

  C.

Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA).

  D.

Policy development for USP 800 implementation.

*Question 24:

The Department of Health and The Joint Commission are expected to survey your institution in the next 6–12 months. The clinical manager is concerned that the institution may be at risk of citations related to safe medication use. Which tool would best help assess your institution’s performance on safe medication use?

  A.

Institute for Safe Medication Practices (ISMP) Targeted Medication Safety Best Practices for Hospitals worksheet.

  B.

Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle.

  C.

Gap analysis of Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) core measures.

  D.

Six Sigma: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control (DMAIC) process.

*Question 25:

A 48-year-old woman presents to the emergency department overnight with a traumatic brain injury after an unhelmeted motorcycle accident. Her initial head CT reveals a large subdural hematoma. The neurosurgeon is concerned for intracranial hypertension and tries to order hypertonic saline (HTS) using the computerized clinician order entry (CPOE) system. Many concentrations are available, including 3%, 5%, 7.5%, and 23.4% HTS, with varying volumes. The provider, unsure which to select, submits an order for 50 mL of 23.4% HTS. The covering pharmacist calls the provider and states that 23.4% HTS cannot be dispensed to patient care areas according to formulary restrictions. . The covering pharmacist then helps the neurosurgeon order the correct formulary concentration and volume, 150 mL of 5% HTS. The attending neurosurgeon requests a better process for selecting and ordering HTS. You would like to create a guideline outlining appropriate use of HTS in addition to a new CPOE order set to facilitate ordering. Which would best be considered when developing a guideline and new order panel for HTS prescribing?​​

  A.

Identify the key stakeholders involved, including the target users of the guideline and order panel, to assist in creation.

  B.

The guideline can be created according to provider preference without consideration of supporting literature or guidelines.

  C.

It is not necessary to obtain approvals beyond the workgroup developing the guideline.

  D.

The guideline can be vague if it includes the formulary HTS concentrations available.

*Question 26:

New pharmacy transitions of care service was implemented in which a clinical pharmacist conducts medication profile reviews for all patients transferred from the intensive care unit (ICU) to a lower level of care within 24 hours, with the goal of improving medication safety and decreasing ICU readmission. Which metric would best assess the effectiveness of this service and potentially justify additional full-time equivalents (FTEs) to support the service?

  A.

Hospital mortality.

  B.

Number and impact of pharmacist interventions.

  C.

ICU mortality.

  D.

Number of medication reconciliations performed.

*Question 27:

Time to antibiotics for patients with sepsis is falling out of compliance with a median time to administration of 85 minutes. The nurse manager of your intensive care unit asks you to help decrease this time to less than 60 minutes. From a pharmacy perspective, a process map was created surrounding the workflow related to antibiotic verification, intravenous preparation, and delivery. Which best depicts a LEAN principle that can be used to identify current workflow vulnerabilities in the process map that outlines the steps from order entry to administration of a stat antibiotic, to target intervention?​​

  A.

Create a value stream map.

  B.

Perform a Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA).

  C.

Perform the Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control (DMAIC) process.

  D.

Identify “downtime” wastes.

*Question 28:

A medication use evaluation (MUE) performed at your institution evaluated the use of vasopressin infusions, given the high cost to the health system. It was discovered that the use of vasopressin varies from patient to patient and across service lines, including variations in initial dose, dose titrations versus flat dosing, discontinuation practices, duration, concentration, and place in therapy. For example, in one unit, it was discovered that most patients had vasopressin tapered from 0.04 units/minute, where the taper to off lasted, on average, 72 hours. To standardize use to help contain costs, which course of action would be best?​​ 

  A.

Create a policy outlining acceptable use of vasopressin.

  B.

Provide education on how to use vasopressin more consistently.

  C.

Develop a clinical guideline for the use of vasopressin.

  D.

Perform a root-cause analysis to investigate why the taper of vasopressin to off took 72 hours.

*Question 29:

Minor/moderate adverse events related to insulin administration for the treatment of hyperkalemia have increasingly been entered into the organization’s event reporting system. The event reports indicate that some patients receiving insulin plus dextrose in the setting of hyperkalemia become hypoglycemic and require additional administration of dextrose. Which would best evaluate insulin administration for the treatment of hyperkalemia to determine the course of action to take?            

  A.

Evaluate the Institute for Safe Medication Practices (ISMP) Targeted Medication Safety Best Practices for Hospitals and perform a gap analysis.

  B.

Develop a policy for the use of insulin for the treatment of hyperkalemia.

  C.

Perform a medication use evaluation (MUE) on insulin administration for the treatment of hyperkalemia.

  D.

Document pharmacist interventions when a patient receives insulin for the treatment of hyperkalemia and develops hypoglycemia.

*Question 30:

A man admitted to the neurology intensive care unit with status epilepticus was stabilized with the following regimen: phenytoin, levetiracetam, valproic acid, and clobazam. His stay was complicated by acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring intubation for the past 12 days. The patient became febrile overnight and required an increase in ventilator requirements and fraction of inspired oxygen; meropenem and vancomycin were initiated, and the patient had two seizures last night. After reviewing his profile this morning, you alert the team to the meropenem and valproic acid drug-drug interaction that could be responsible for his most recent seizures. You document this intervention and the adverse drug event. The medication safety officer at your institution reaches out and recommends performing a medication use evaluation (MUE) to determine the incidence of this error and identify opportunities for improvement. Which best describes the step in the MUE process that incorporates the “Five Whys” to identify variation in the prescribing process that could result in this error?​

  A.

Act.

  B.

Check.

  C.

Clarify.

  D.

Understand.

Pharmacoeconomics and Safe Medication Use

*Question 31:

Your institution wants to add filgrastim-sndz (a biosimilar) to the formulary as an alternative to filgrastim. Data support that patient outcomes are similar between the 2 formulations. The advantage is that filgrastim-sndz costs less than filgrastim. Which type of economic analysis is best to provide convincing evidence that filgrastim-sndz is an appropriate addition to the formulary from an institutional perspective?

  A.

Cost-benefit.

  B.

Cost-effectiveness.

  C.

Cost-minimization.

  D.

Cost-utility.

*Question 32:

Your pharmacy department is interested in evaluating the use of icatibant for acute exacerbations of hereditary angioedema, compared with C1 esterase inhibitor (human). According to limited supporting data, which type of economic analysis would be best for your institution to perform?

  A.

Cost-benefit.

  B.

Cost-effectiveness.

  C.

Cost-minimization.

  D.

Cost-utility.

*Question 33:

A 70-year-old patient is admitted to the medical ICU for the management of respiratory failure secondary to pneumonia requiring intubation. On hospital day 3, the pneumonia is being appropriately treated with antimicrobials, and the patient has been afebrile for 24 hours. Dexmedetomidine is initiated to prepare the patient for extubation. Within your institution’s guidelines, a dose of 0.4 μg/kg/h is initiated. Now, 12 hours later, the nurse reports that the patient has developed a new temperature of 39.2 °C, and acetaminophen is administered. No other causes of fever are identified. Which best categorizes this incident?

  A.

Adverse drug reaction (ADR).

  B.

Medication error.

  C.

Preventable adverse drug event (ADE).

  D.

Preventable ADR.

*Question 34:

Cardiovascular Critical Care I

The next two questions pertain to the following case.

A.C. is a 62-year-old woman who presents to the ED with chief concerns of nausea, vomiting, and shortness of breath that have persisted for 3 days. The initial ECG reveals ST-segment elevations in leads V1 and V2, prompting aspirin 324 mg orally, ticagrelor 180 mg orally, and an intravenous heparin bolus and infusion at 16 units/kg/h. The patient has a medical history of type 2 diabetes and only takes metformin 500 mg twice daily at home. Her ejection fraction at a cardiology visit 7 months ago was 54%. Her initial vital signs are blood pressure 84/48 mm Hg despite receiving a 1-L normal saline bolus, heart rate 90 to 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and Sao2 93% on 4 L of O2. Her physical examination is significant for labored respirations, diffuse crackles bilaterally, 3+ lower extremity edema bilaterally, and cool and dry extremities. A bedside ECHO reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) estimated at less than 20% with hypokinesis of the anterior left ventricular wall. Chest radiography reveals bilateral pulmonary vascular congestion and no pulmonary infiltrates. Add vasopressin.

*Question 114:

A 45-year-old man (weight 80 kg) without a significant medical history presents to the ED with lethargy and several gunshot wounds. His estimated blood loss is 2000 mL. Platelets and tranexamic acid.

FFP, platelets, and cryoprecipitate.

Loss of oxygen-carrying capacity because of low hemoglobin.

Toxicology

*Question 143:

A 39-year-old man presents to the ED after sustaining a fall, resulting in a left hip dislocation. After radiologically confirming the dislocation, the health care team plans to perform a procedural sedation, reposition the hip correctly, and discharge the patient from the ED. For this procedure, the senior physician chooses intravenous propofol and fentanyl. Administration of both agents achieves adequate sedation, and another physician repositions the hip. The patient is minimally agitated during the procedure but tolerates it well. After the procedure, however, the patient’s Sao2 begins to decrease to 90%, and the respiratory therapist at the bedside applies a jaw thrust. The patient is minimally arousable to commands but fully responsive to sternal pressure. After 10 minutes with no change in the patient’s condition, the physician consults you for naloxone therapy. Which naloxone route and dose is most appropriate at this time?

  A.

*Question 144:

A 65-year-old man is brought to the ED after being found at a bus stop with altered mental status. On hospital arrival, the patient is jittery and tremulous but awake and not in acute distress. Intravenous access is obtained, blood samples are obtained, and the patient is intravenously administered 1000 mL of lactated Ringer solution. On questioning, the patient admits regularly drinking about 1 pt of liquor daily; however, his last drink was about 24 hours ago. While being questioned about his medical history, the patient begins to have a tonic-clonic seizure lasting more than 5 minutes. Lorazepam 4 mg intravenously is administered, after which he stops seizing but becomes groggy. Presuming this patient is experiencing severe alcohol withdrawal, which agent is best to administer next to treat the symptoms and prevent further seizure activity?

Chlordiazepoxide 100 mg orally.

  B.

Midazolam 4 mg intravenously.

  C.

Diazepam 10 mg intravenously.

  D.

Baclofen 10 mg orally.

Atropine 1-mg intravenous bolus.

Dobutamine 2-μg/kg/min intravenous infusion.

Recommend completing a 5-day course of the current methylprednisolone regimen.

C.

Change methylprednisolone to prednisone 40 mg by enteral tube daily for 5 days total.

D.

Recommend adding magnesium sulfate 2 g as an intravenous piggyback × 1 dose.

Toxicology

Question 143:

A 39-year-old man presents to the ED after sustaining a fall, resulting in a left hip dislocation. After radiologically confirming the dislocation, the health care team plans to perform a procedural sedation, reposition the hip correctly, and discharge the patient from the ED. For this procedure, the senior physician chooses intravenous propofol and fentanyl. Administration of both agents achieves adequate sedation, and another physician repositions the hip. The patient is minimally agitated during the procedure but tolerates it well. After the procedure, however, the patient’s Sao2 begins to decrease to 90%, and the respiratory therapist at the bedside applies a jaw thrust. The patient is minimally arousable to commands but fully responsive to sternal pressure. After 10 minutes with no change in the patient’s condition, the physician consults you for naloxone therapy. Which naloxone route and dose is most appropriate at this time?

A.

0.04 mg intravenously.

B.

2 mg intravenously.

C.

2 mg intramuscularly.

D.

0.04 mg intramuscularly.

Question 144:

A 65-year-old man is brought to the ED after being found at a bus stop with altered mental status. On hospital arrival, the patient is jittery and tremulous but awake and not in acute distress. Intravenous access is obtained, blood samples are obtained, and the patient is intravenously administered 1000 mL of lactated Ringer solution. On questioning, the patient admits regularly drinking about 1 pt of liquor daily; however, his last drink was about 24 hours ago. While being questioned about his medical history, the patient begins to have a tonic-clonic seizure lasting more than 5 minutes. Lorazepam 4 mg intravenously is administered, after which he stops seizing but becomes groggy. Presuming this patient is experiencing severe alcohol withdrawal, which agent is best to administer next to treat the symptoms and prevent further seizure activity?

A.

Chlordiazepoxide 100 mg orally.

B.

Midazolam 4 mg intravenously.

C.

Diazepam 10 mg intravenously.

D.

Baclofen 10 mg orally.

Question 145:

A 66-year-old man presents to the ED because of substantial fatigue and drowsiness. The patient has a medical history of a 4-vessel coronary artery bypass graft surgery. His current medications are metoprolol extended release, aspirin, clopidogrel, and alprazolam. His vital signs are blood pressure, 82/40 mm Hg; heart rate, 31 beats/min; respiratory rate, 25 breaths/min; and temperature, 37.1 °C. The health care team suspects this patient is experiencing chronic β-blocker toxicity. Which recommendation is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

A.

Glucagon 10-mg intravenous bolus.

B.

Regular insulin 1-unit/kg intravenous bolus.

C.

Atropine 1-mg intravenous bolus.

D.

Dobutamine 2-μg/kg/min intravenous infusion.

Question 146:

A 39-year-old woman presents to the ED after being found unresponsive, but arousable, by her family about 90 minutes ago. On arrival, she is somnolent, groggy, and minimally responsive to voice and pain. Her medical history is significant for depression and suicidal ideation. An empty bottle of clonazepam 0.5 mg was found next to her that was filled 2 days ago for 60 pills. Her vital signs on arrival are blood pressure, 100/65 mm Hg; heart rate, 76 beats/min; respiratory rate, 10 breaths/min; and temperature, 36.7 °C The health care team consults you regarding options for gastric decontamination. Which recommendation is most appropriate for this patient?

A.

Administer gastric lavage with 10-mL/kg aliquots of sterile water.

B.

Administer magnesium citrate 4 mL/kg.

C.

Administer activated charcoal 50 g.

D.

Gastric decontamination is not recommended.

Question 147:

A 36-year-old man with an unknown medical history presents to the ED after being found walking in the middle of the street by bystanders. On arrival at the ED, his vital signs are blood pressure 142/96 mm Hg, heart rate 128 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and temperature 37.9 °C. On further questioning, the patient admits taking oxycodone and “molly” or MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine) last night. He is severely agitated and threatening staff. The health care team suspects toxicity secondary to his stimulant ingestion. Which recommendation is most appropriate for managing the sympathetic symptoms?

A.

Ziprasidone 10 mg intramuscularly.

B.

Lorazepam 1 mg intravenously.

C.

Olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly.

D.

Haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly.

Question 148:

A 55-year-old woman presents to the ED with acute altered mental status. She is somnolent, but responsive to stimuli, and reports that she ingested multiple medications, including more than 10 g of acetaminophen, in an apparent suicide attempt. She is unable to recall when the ingestion occurred and was last seen by her family about 8 hours before presentation. A review of her medical history in the electronic medical record shows previous suicide attempts with acetaminophen. Her vital signs are blood pressure, 102/56 mm Hg; heart rate, 76 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; and temperature, 37.3 °C. Laboratory samples have been obtained, but the results are not yet available. The health care team consults you regarding how to approach possible antidotal therapy. Which recommendation is best at this time?

A.

Acetylcysteine is not indicated until the results of the acetaminophen concentration are known.

B.

Administer activated charcoal 50 g initially, followed by 50 g every 4 hours.

C.

Administer oral acetylcysteine 140-mg/kg bolus.

D.

Administer intravenous acetylcysteine 150-mg/kg bolus.

Question 149:

A 72-year-old woman presents to the ED with concerns for profound weakness and bradycardia. Emergency medical services administered 1 mg of atropine intravenously en route with a minimal response. On arrival, the patient’s heart rate is 42 beats/min and blood pressure is 95/52 mm Hg. Her medical history is significant for recent electrical cardioversion for new-onset atrial fibrillation and initiation of diltiazem extended release 180 mg/d. The health care team consults you regarding which therapies are most appropriate for the treatment of her symptomatic bradycardia. Which recommendation is most appropriate at this time?

A.

Calcium gluconate 3-g intravenous bolus.

B.

Glucagon 10-mg intravenous bolus.

C.

20% intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5-mL/kg intravenous bolus.

D.

Regular insulin 1-unit/kg intravenous bolus.

Question 150:

A 49-year-old man presents to the ED with acute onset of dizziness on standing. Physical evaluation reveals orthostatic hypotension on standing. Lactated Ringer solution 2000 mL intravenously is administered with minimal symptom relief. His medical history is significant for depression. He was recently initiated on desipramine 200 mg/d; however, on further questioning, he admits he had been taking it twice daily whenever he “felt down.” His blood pressure is now 110/86 mm Hg when seated and heart rate is 68 beats/min. An ECG reveals a normal QTc and a QRS of 140 milliseconds. Which intervention is most appropriate to implement?

A.

Magnesium 2-g intravenous bolus.

B.

Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 1-mEq/kg intravenous bolus. 

C.

20% intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5-mL/kg intravenous bolus.

D.

Dopamine 5-μg/kg/min intravenous infusion.
